newsitem.title: BOSNIA: U.S. envoy pushes for deal on Bosnian c.bank.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy pushes for deal on Bosnian c.bank.

text.p: A high level U.S. delegation lobbied Bosnia's Moslem, Croat and Serb leaders on Wednesday in an attempt to resolve a long-running dispute over the formation of a single central bank.
U.S. envoy Robert Gelbard held talks with members of the collective presidency to push for an agreement on the central bank law, foreign experts said.

"It is a source of enormous frustration to me and my government that the parties and the government of this country have so far been unable and unwilling to take the necessary steps to help and ensure a better life for their people," Gelbard told reporters upon arrival on Tuesday.

Gelbard, accompanied by officials from the U.S. Treasury Department and the International Monetary Fund (IMF), was trying to secure an agreement in time for the scheduled visit of Secretary of State Madeleine Albright this weekend.

Bosnian leaders have been squabbling over the issue for the past six months, forcing the postponement of a donors' conference for reconstruction and blocking a crucial agreement with the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
The U.S.-brokered peace treaty which ended the 1992-95 war in Bosnia divided the country into autonomous Serb and Moslem-Croat entities ruled by a small central government.
The joint presidency, cabinet and parliament have fallen into a stalemate over virtually every major issue, including the proposed central bank law.
Nationalist Serb authorities, who fought against Bosnian statehood, have been reluctant to accept a single central bank as envisaged by the peace accord.
Gelbard's first priority was to persuade Bosnian leaders to reaffirm their commitment to a preliminary agreement brokered by U.S. officials on April 15, foreign experts said.
Under that accord, presidency members pledged their support for a single central bank and currency and proposed issuing temporary coupons until a currency design could be agreed.

"The delegation will not be happy with anything else than a reaffirmed April 15 agreement and a signed central bank law, which simply reflects the agreement's principles," the analyst, who asked not to named, said.
The April 15 agreement was never signed and U.S. officials wanted to ensure the politicians stuck to their word, he said.

"They want to see it in writing and signed in blood because the April 15 agreement on the central bank was not signed and therefore it opened the door to many issues we thought were resolved," he said.
"It's flip a coin and see. There is some optimism that it can be done but then again the realities of the Balkans tell us to be cautious," the analyst said.
The IMF agreement with Bosnia would not only bring $100 million in aid but would reassure foreign investors that the country had adopted basic economic reforms.

Apart from the central bank law, the IMF has also called for an agreement on the new currency and a timetable for its introduction, budget laws, uniform tariffs and a law on servicing of Bosnia's external debt.
Most of the IMF conditions were close to being fulfilled except the central bank law, experts said. Resolving the dispute would clear the way for a donors' conference in late June or early July.
World Bank officials hope to raise some $1.4 billion in reconstruction aid for 1997 at the conference.
